proxy_language: Proto-Austronesian / Proto-Austroasiatic / Proto-Hmong-Mien / Proto-Tai-Kadai (regional composite, anchored on Old Chinese Baxter-Sagart notation for pan-Sinitic forms and Proto-Hmong-Mien for the Yangtze)
proxy_rationale: Yuchanyan (Hunan, c. 18-14k BP, earliest pottery) and Xianrendong (Jiangxi, c. 20-10k BP) are known only archaeologically; the languages of their foragers are unrecoverable and almost certainly extinct without descendants. The middle Yangtze is the proposed homeland region for Hmong-Mien (Ratliff 2010, Sagart) and a candidate zone for early Austroasiatic/Tai-Kadai contact, while Sagart places Austronesian ancestors on the coast. The link is geographically plausible but chronologically 10k+ years too deep, so Proto-Hmong-Mien-style phonotactics (monosyllabic roots with tone, initial clusters absent or limited, prenasalized stops) are used as the principal model, with Old Chinese-style sesquisyllables as an alternative texture.
phonology: Modelled on Proto-Hmong-Mien (Ratliff 2010): stops p t c k q with voiced/prenasalized counterparts (b d dz g, mp nt nk), fricatives s h z, nasals m n ny ng, liquids l, glides w y, vowels i e a o u plus diphthongs ai au ei ou. Contrastive tones (four to eight) are omitted from spelling; they are mapped to simple syllable-final letters at most. No claim is made that this reflects Yuchanyan speech.
phonotactics: Predominantly monosyllabic roots of shape (C)(C)V(V)(N), where final C is limited to a nasal (n, ng, m) or a glottal or tonal marker; no final obstruent clusters; initial clusters limited to prenasal+stop (mp, nt, nk, mb, nd, ng) or stop+glide (ky, ty, py, kw, tw). Compound names are built from two or three syllables, each a separate morpheme. Vowel-initial syllables are rare and take a glottal onset.
orthography: Practical Latin transliteration in the style of Hmong RPA/Pinyin hybrid without tone letters: plosives p t k, affricates c (ts-like) and q (palatal), ny, ng, ts, sh, x omitted. Hyphens separate morphemes in compounds; apostrophe is not used. Vowels a e i o u, diphthongs ai au ei ou ia ua.
morphology: Isolating: roots are free monosyllables with little or no affixation. Number and definiteness are expressed by classifiers and demonstratives (Hmong-Mien classifier systems are rich, e.g. Hmong tus for animals, lub for rounded objects). Derivation is by compounding, occasional tonal change, and a few prefixes (a- as a nominal prefix in Hmong-Mien and Sino-Tibetan areal usage). No case, no gender.
compounding: Modifier-head or head-modifier both occur in the area; Proto-Hmong-Mien and Tai-Kadai favour head-initial noun phrases (noun then modifier), while Chinese and some Mien varieties show modifier-head. For gameplay a consistent head-initial model is used: 'X of Y' = X Y juxtaposed (head noun first, possessor second) without linker; 'Y-maker' = verb+noun or noun+classifier+agent compound; place names = feature word + descriptor (river/mountain/cave + quality).
noun_phrase_order: Head noun first, then modifiers: Noun + Adjective, Noun + Possessor, Noun + Demonstrative; numerals and classifiers precede the noun (Num + Clf + N), as in Hmong-Mien and Tai-Kadai.

attested_roots.gloss: rice plant, rice (Proto-Hmong-Mien root for paddy/rice)
water, river (areal root, cf. Austroasiatic *ʔɗaːk and Hmong-Mien *ʔwɔm)
pot, vessel (Hmong-Mien and Chinese areal word, cf. Old Chinese *tˤoŋ)

sources: Ratliff, Martha. Hmong-Mien Language History (Pacific Linguistics, 2010)
Baxter, William H. and Laurent Sagart. Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction (2014)
Sagart, Laurent. The Roots of Old Chinese (1999)
Sagart, Blench and Sanchez-Mazas (eds). The Peopling of East Asia (2005)
Wu Xiaohong et al. 'Early pottery at 20,000 years ago in Xianrendong Cave, China', Science 336 (2012)
notes: Highly speculative: the actual language(s) of Yuchanyan and Xianrendong foragers are unknown, and any link to Hmong-Mien or other modern families is geographically suggestive only. Names should sound plausibly East/Southeast Asian in a monosyllabic, tone-less transliteration, not claim to be real attested words. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word, as this is not a Goidelic culture. The reconstructed forms above are approximate and should be treated as model shapes rather than citable reconstructions.
unit: Early pottery foragers of S China and the Yangtze (Yuchanyan, Xianrendong)
